DV DT Protection Check: Step by Step Method

DV DT protection means keeping both the peak voltage and the rate of voltage rise at the motor terminals inside the limits the winding insulation can handle. The check below uses the critical length formula and the worked values already given in this article for a 480 V drive.

  1. Find the drive output rise time tr. Modern IGBTs switch in roughly 50 to 400 ns.
  2. Calculate the critical length: lc ≈ v × tr ÷ 2, with v about 150 m per µs. For tr = 0.1 µs, lc = 7.5 m.
  3. Compare the real cable length with lc. Beyond lc the full reflection develops and the peak can reach about twice the DC bus voltage.
  4. Estimate the peak. A 480 V drive has a DC bus of about 650 V, so the peak can exceed 1300 V.
  5. Compare with the motor rating. NEMA MG1 Part 31 inverter duty motors withstand about 1600 V peak with rise times of 0.1 µs or longer.
  6. Select the protection from the cable length and motor type, then mount it close to the VFD output.
ItemTypical value from this article
dv/dt guideline, 480 V systemAbout 1000 V per µs
Unfiltered dv/dt, 1300 V in 0.1 µs13000 V per µs
Rise time needed for 1000 V per µsAbout 1.3 µs
Output reactorShort runs under about 300 ft
dv/dt filterRuns of about 300 to 1000 ft
Sine wave filterVery long runs and submersible pumps

Older motors without inverter duty insulation need the strictest protection, because their first turns fail from partial discharge long before the thermal limit is reached.
